title: Why AI Will Create More Legal Work, Not Less: Filevine's Rizner and Anderson on Research, Access, and Human Judgment
author: Ryan Anderson · John Rizner

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source overlaps with the cluster by depicting a rapidly widening, harder-to-navigate legal-technology ecosystem, including competition between big-tech platforms and specialist tools. Its principal emphasis, however, is a different proposition: that lower-cost AI-enabled services may expand legal demand through the Jevons paradox. It does not substantively assess workflow fit, adoption, renewal economics, consumption costs or realized procurement value.
qs: Instead of asking how many legal jobs AI will destroy, we’re actually going to explore why AI may actually trigger an unprecedented explosion of legal work, opening up massive markets that were historically priced out.
It was already a tough market to navigate when all you had to worry about were the thousands of legal applications; now you also need to track what’s happening in the broader tech ecosystem.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: The source excerpt contains only contact information and listener outreach, with no substantive claims about organisational adaptation, human control, legal work, pricing, employment or AI adoption. It therefore provides insufficient evidence to assess a position relative to the cluster proposition.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source identifies growing product-selection complexity and promises a future comparison of big-tech legal offerings, but it does not take a clear position on practitioner-led experimentation, redesign before technological certainty, shared implementation, reliability, access to justice, or judicial legitimacy.
qs: It was already a tough market to navigate when all you had to worry about were the thousands of legal applications; now you also need to track what’s happening in the broader tech ecosystem.
We’ll soon be publishing a helpful comparison of the big tech offerings for legal, with an examination of where in the legal tech stack they might be useful.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s emphasis on human judgment, controlled use and redesigned training, and materially extends it by identifying model-specific jurisprudential assumptions as an implementation risk: different model families may produce different legal recommendations, so institutional absorption should include model selection, playbooks and guidance for junior users.
qs: What was maybe surprising, maybe unsurprising, was that depending on what model or what family of models you were using, you could see dramatically different results on whether the LLM was pushing the judge or the practitioner to push for a breach of contract or to keep a promise.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s emphasis on frontline experimentation and multidisciplinary implementation, while materially extending it by arguing that lower-cost exploration can improve legal creativity, not merely efficiency. Its lawyer-research and live-prototyping examples are anecdotal and do not establish organisation-wide transformation or address resistance, incentives and leadership.
qs: But I think great lawyers are exceptionally creative, and by lowering the cost to go on a creative thread with a legal theory, you enable much more creativity.

Does anyone want to see what I just did?” And we literally shared a screen, and he showed something — not in a production environment, but on his local machine using real live code — and said, “Here’s how I think we should do it.” It was working, and we could actually play with it right there during the meeting.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Filevine accepts the cluster’s human-led, selective-deployment model: AI can expand and improve bounded legal work, but persuasive errors, model-dependent outcomes and hallucinations preserve the need for legal judgment and supervision. It materially develops the proposition by specifying a three-part citation-verification framework—existence, proposition support and continuing validity—and by arguing that lower production costs may expand legal activity rather than simply eliminate labour.
qs: AI tools are very important, but they have to be watched over, for sure.
And on the third level is that citational analysis: okay, the opinion exists, it supports what you care about — now, is it good law in the larger common law analysis?

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s claims that legal quality is not reducible to a single model answer and that human checkpoints remain necessary. Its reported model-family differences reinforce the difficulty of evaluating substantive legal recommendations, while its emphasis on nuanced errors and human judgment supports continued expert oversight; it does not independently establish the broader workflow-design proposition.
qs: What was maybe surprising, maybe unsurprising, was that depending on what model or what family of models you were using, you could see dramatically different results on whether the LLM was pushing the judge or the practitioner to push for a breach of contract or to keep a promise.
But we’re huge believers in the primacy of human judgment when it comes to the law.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central competence concern: AI outputs require experienced human verification, while juniors may overrely on them and learn from defective work. It also endorses structured guidance such as playbooks and templates, but does not substantively address the loss of traditional apprenticeship work or develop a broader replacement training model.
qs: Someone who’s got more extensive experience would look at this and automatically say, “Absolutely not.” But somebody who’s more junior, and who’s actually using this as a learning tool in addition to a drafting tool, is really going down the wrong path.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: Shaver supports the cluster’s emphasis on informed filtering: she argues that legal-technology buyers must monitor developments beyond legal-specific products and assess where big-tech offerings fit in the legal technology stack. Her announced comparison is a proposed filtering aid, not evidence that any particular selection method improves outcomes.
qs: It was already a tough market to navigate when all you had to worry about were the thousands of legal applications; now you also need to track what’s happening in the broader tech ecosystem.
We’ll soon be publishing a helpful comparison of the big tech offerings for legal, with an examination of where in the legal tech stack they might be useful.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s qualified account: AI can reduce production or exploration costs, but human verification remains necessary and the billable hour may persist rather than yield to a single replacement model. Its examples are anecdotal and it does not materially develop end-to-end delivery redesign or the apprenticeship problem.
qs: AI tools are very important, but they have to be watched over, for sure.

John Rizner (24:09) I think, on the one hand, the billable hour has survived a lot of technological change so far and has not disappeared yet, so I think the billable hour has some weight to it that will be hard to remove.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s framing of AI as an expertise-development and supervision challenge rather than straightforward lawyer substitution. It specifically warns that junior users may mistake AI output for sound instruction and stresses enduring legal judgment and verification, while offering no evidence that automation has already transformed succession or employment.
qs: Someone who’s got more extensive experience would look at this and automatically say, “Absolutely not.” But somebody who’s more junior, and who’s actually using this as a learning tool in addition to a drafting tool, is really going down the wrong path.
AI tools are very important, but they have to be watched over, for sure.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: Shaver supports the cluster’s market-facing proposition that specialist legal-AI vendors now compete or coexist with broader technology platforms, making purchasing decisions more complex. She identifies the replacement-versus-complement question and urges buyers to track the wider technology ecosystem, but does not address the cluster’s claims about lawyer guidance, workflow redesign or verification.
qs: Ever since Anthropic launched Claude for Legal, a lot of focus has been on whether firms and legal departments should be using that in place of, or as well as, legal-specific applications like Harvey and Legora.
It was already a tough market to navigate when all you had to worry about were the thousands of legal applications; now you also need to track what’s happening in the broader tech ecosystem.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source supports selective augmentation: AI can improve research discovery and deepen legal analysis, but persuasive outputs may contain consequential errors, so lawyers must retain judgment and examine authorities themselves. Its claims about improved work quality are mainly predictive and anecdotal rather than measured.
qs: It is one thing to see an AI output as an unsophisticated consumer of that information and say, “Geez, this kind of looks pretty good and pretty persuasive.” But I think all of us have seen enough AI results and prompts and, frankly, slop to go: hold on, hold on — this looks like it’s right, but it is in fact not right, and sometimes in really critical but perhaps nuanced ways.
But we’re huge believers in the primacy of human judgment when it comes to the law.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI will automate and compress parts of legal production while preserving the need for lawyers’ judgment, oversight and accountability. It also aligns with the cluster’s qualified demand-expansion and access-to-justice claims, predicting greater lawyer capacity while recognising verification and court-capacity constraints. Its claims are largely predictive and anecdotal rather than evidence of market-wide restructuring.
qs: So the legal judgment to know the difference between what is close and what is precise is going to be needed for a long time.
And it’s pretty awesome that lawyers are going to have much more capacity now.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition that AI task substitution can complement lawyers and expand the amount or depth of substantive work rather than mechanically reducing labour demand. It predicts that easier research discovery will lead lawyers to review more material and develop more nuanced arguments, while offering only anecdotal preferences and forecasts—not measured staffing or employment outcomes.
qs: So I think as AI tools, especially in the legal research space, the citator space, make finding the relevant literature easier — even making more of the relevant literature an immediate delivery to the user — rather than lawyers spending less time doing research, we’re going to see lawyers spend more time doing substantive research.

The difference being, instead of lawyers saying, “All right, I’ve got X amount of time, I found this handful of cases, let’s quickly draft this and get it out the door,” I think you’re going to see far more in-depth and nuanced arguments in legal work product, due to the fact that lawyers will have easier access to greater amounts of research material.

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition that an expanding legal-AI market complicates selection. It identifies big-tech entry as an additional layer buyers must monitor and frames comparison by fit within the legal-tech stack, while offering no comparative performance evidence or recommendation.
qs: It was already a tough market to navigate when all you had to worry about were the thousands of legal applications; now you also need to track what’s happening in the broader tech ecosystem.

Ever since Anthropic launched Claude for Legal, a lot of focus has been on whether firms and legal departments should be using that in place of, or as well as, legal-specific applications like Harvey and Legora.

st.t: Workflow trust: Verification remains costly and contested
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core framing that trust depends on supervised workflows rather than error-free AI. It cites fabricated testimony language and model-dependent judgment as reasons for continued lawyer verification, while also recognizing that adoption follows incentives and that hourly billing may obstruct efficiency gains.
qs: AI tools are very important, but they have to be watched over, for sure.
So John, Greg and I saw your presentation at Texas Trailblazers a few months back, and you noted that AI adoption follows incentives, and that trust in AI is ultimately a workflow problem.

kp.k: Cheaper research could increase research depth and legal work
kp.d: Asked about Jevons paradox, John Rizner predicts that easier access to relevant authorities will increase substantive research rather than simply reduce research time. His supporting evidence is conversations with former law-school classmates who became appellate litigators and wanted to exhaust more materials if resources permitted. He anticipates more nuanced arguments and better judicial opinions; these are predictions, not measured quality improvements.
qs: What was interesting is all of them said, actually, if I had unlimited time and unlimited resources, I would want to find more and read more, as opposed to find less and read less.
rather than lawyers spending less time doing research, we’re going to see lawyers spend more time doing substantive research.
So volume may grow, and in addition to volume growing, I think quality becomes far better in the long run.

kp.k: Engineering provides an analogy for expanding professional demand
kp.d: Ryan Anderson reports that Filevine writes at least ten times as much code as before, while reviewing, testing and maintaining an expanding product generates additional work. He expects year-end engineering employment of approximately 400–450, about half ML engineers. He uses this company experience and his asserted industry hiring recovery from post-COVID lows as an analogy for legal demand expansion, rather than presenting legal employment evidence.
qs: I think we will end the year with something like 400 to 450 engineers, about half of which are ML engineers, the other half your traditional coders.
We definitely write 10 times more code today than we did before — it might even be more than 10 times more.
But for every piece of code that we write, it has to be reviewed, it has to be QA’d, it has to be tested.
And as the aperture of the product increases, the surface area for problems increases, but the ambition of the product also grows.

kp.k: Lower litigation costs could stimulate reciprocal procedural work
kp.d: Anderson predicts that cheaper, faster drafting will make previously unaffordable motions and witness discovery worthwhile. Because litigation requires counterparties to respond, additional activity on one side could generate further activity on the other. He expects increased litigation, including employment disputes, without claiming that every resulting claim will be meritorious. He also relays customer accounts of LOIS revealing unexpected legal theories as anecdotal support for cheaper creative exploration.
qs: But boy, now that you can bring that motion to compel, and it’s much easier to draft and much quicker, the opportunity costs change, and the search for truth becomes sort of superpowered.
And of course, litigation in particular is a counterparty affair — what one side does, the other side is having to respond to, and then maybe bringing a counterattack themselves.
When you lower the cost for exploration, for creative exploration, people become much more creative.
But yes, I think you can expect an increase in litigation across the board.

kp.k: Expanded capacity could serve previously unmet legal needs
kp.d: Anderson predicts greater service availability in family law, immigration and bankruptcy, alongside better representation for underrepresented criminal defendants and more opportunities to challenge wrongful prosecutions or inadequate representation. His access argument includes an anecdote about his well-connected brother struggling to secure help with a small real-estate dispute. Illustrative will-drafting time reductions suggest lower total client bills and greater throughput without necessarily lowering hourly rates; he acknowledges uncertainty about how this unfolds.
qs: If you’re somebody who’s indigent, working class, maybe you don’t grow up with the same kind of privileges or connections, it can be extremely challenging to find good legal representation.

I think you’ll see a lot more in family law, a lot more immigration law, a lot more bankruptcy, and I think underrepresented criminal defendants are going to be in much better shape than they are today.

You don’t even have to reduce your rates that much — maybe your rates stay the same, they might even go higher — but you’re able to serve more people, and those people wind up paying less because they’re taking less of the lawyer’s time.
We don’t know exactly how it will all play out, but more legal customers will be served than ever before.

kp.k: Court capacity could constrain gains in legal access
kp.d: Host Greg Lambert warns that increased plaintiff and defendant efficiency will not deliver access if courts cannot absorb the influx of cases. Anderson likewise anticipates difficulty for judges. Responding to the hosts' suggestions about AI dispute resolution, he predicts some consensual AI use in small private arbitrations, while rejecting the near-term replacement of judges and lawyers.
qs: if we don’t figure out how they are going to handle this massive influx of new cases, it doesn’t matter really how much of the efficiency gets on the plaintiff/defendant side if the court system is inaccessible.
I think you can envision small arbitrations that are private, where at least they agree to maybe some AI tooling being used.
So I think we’re a very far ways off from lawyers being replaced, from judges being replaced.

kp.k: Human verification remains essential despite persuasive AI outputs
kp.d: Anderson argues that apparently convincing outputs can contain consequential, nuanced errors requiring legal judgment. He reports a customer's comparison in which Claude presented an amalgamation of witness statements as a literal quotation. This is a vendor-relayed incident, not a comparative error-rate study. His endorsement of continuing human oversight accompanies an explicit acknowledgment that AI products are central to Filevine's business.
qs: We basically only sell LOIS and AI products today, which is quite a difference from where we were three to four years ago.
And it turned out that witness hadn’t said that; it was sort of an amalgamation of three or four things the witness had said.
So the legal judgment to know the difference between what is close and what is precise is going to be needed for a long time.
AI tools are very important, but they have to be watched over, for sure.

kp.k: Higher quality expectations could preserve hourly billing
kp.d: Rizner predicts that the billable hour will survive because lawyers can reinvest saved production time in deeper research and more tailored work. In his hypothetical reduction from eight hours to two for the same output, the remaining six hours support higher, almost partner-level quality. He expects associates to face greater demands for nuance; this is an argument for continued hourly economics, not evidence that firms have already restructured incentives.
qs: the billable hour has survived a lot of technological change so far and has not disappeared yet
The deep nuance that an associate may not have been required or expected to have today will be a requirement in the very near future and in the long run.
So those extra six hours will be spent producing that higher-level, almost partner-level deep quality that just wasn’t accessible or doable today.
So I think the billable hour survives for a while

kp.k: Citator disagreement exposes gaps in single-provider research
kp.d: Rizner cites quantitative research by Paul Hellyer and Susan Mart showing potentially substantial differences in Lexis and Westlaw citation results. He says Filevine's current benchmarking still finds dramatic divergence despite some earlier research dating from eight or five years ago. No sample sizes or numerical disagreement rates are supplied. He argues that cheaper application of multiple methodologies could uncover authorities missed by a single citator; Anderson additionally claims their method finds some cases neither incumbent found.
qs: What’s really interesting is that the differences between the two could be substantial, depending on the opinions looked at.
So if you’re a subscriber only to Westlaw or only to Lexis, you may be missing items that Lexis is returning but Westlaw isn’t, or vice versa.

In our current benchmarking: not so much. Still the dramatic divergence — which citator you happen to be using is going to give you a particular answer, and if you’re using a different one, you’re going to get a different answer.
And we’ve just shown that this method actually picks up a lot of cases that, in some cases, neither of them found.

kp.k: Semantic retrieval targets doctrinal conflicts beyond citation links
kp.d: Rizner describes a LOIS citator approach combining citation graphs and semantic similarity, followed by multiple LLMs assessing relevance and conflict and producing a structured memo. His illustration is Brinkerhoff v. Salt Lake City: he says traditional flags may miss the later rejection of a governmental-immunity doctrine used in its final paragraphs because subsequent authorities need not cite that case. The described LLM panel supports lawyer research rather than exercising judicial authority, and the transcript offers an example rather than quantified validation.
qs: Could we find all of the opinions that could exist and be relevant to the lawyer’s issue?
And then from that, let’s pass that into almost a mock en banc process, where we have a bunch of LLMs operating as judges trying to decide: do we care about these opinions?
What we’re really excited about is finding those opinions that do negatively engage one another but are really hard to find, because they’re not cleanly on a citation graph.
We are able to find these items that are, again, otherwise unfindable on a traditional citation graph.

kp.k: Reliable research requires grounding and three distinct checks
kp.d: Rizner recommends asking vendors which corpora they use, how material reaches models and what benchmarking evidence supports the approach. He describes Filevine's case-file knowledge engine and work using CourtListener's decisions to check citations appearing in LOIS. His three-level framework checks whether an authority exists, supports the asserted proposition and remains good law. He presents coverage of all three levels as a development objective, not an established guarantee of hallucination-free output.
qs: The real question I think lawyers need to be asking their tech providers is: all right, what corpuses are you using? How are you presenting them to your AI technology? And what benchmarks, what kind of evidence do you have that your approach is working well?
On the first level: is this case actually real? Does this citation actually exist somewhere in the corpus?
On the second level, you have that second-order hallucination: does that citation actually refer to and support the proposition you care about?
And on the third level is that citational analysis: okay, the opinion exists, it supports what you care about — now, is it good law in the larger common law analysis?
So that’s how we’re thinking about it: are we building towards hitting all three of those evaluation levels?

kp.k: Word compatibility shapes transactional AI adoption
kp.d: In discussing Filevine's acquisition of Pincites and its rebranding as LOIS for Word, Anderson argues that established document exchange, familiar comments and redlines, and court formatting requirements make Word difficult to displace in the short and medium term. He does not regard it as the inevitable final drafting interface. He describes a product ambition extending beyond redlining to sophisticated long-form documents grounded in evidence and case law.
qs: I don’t think Word is the final surface for all legal drafting, but it is definitely the dominant surface still today
So getting an entire industry to re-platform may be challenging — certainly in the short term, probably in the medium term, maybe not in the long term.
So it’s really not optional, and Word can reliably produce the best-formatted documents for legal in the world.
It is drafting long-form, sophisticated, complex legal documents grounded in evidentiary citations and case law citations.

kp.k: Contract experiments reveal model-dependent substantive legal advice
kp.d: Discussing his co-authored working paper, “The AI’s Philosophy of Contract,” Rizner reports testing then-frontier Anthropic, Google and OpenAI models on large sets of efficient-breach scenarios derived from a human behavioral study. He reports breach recommendations ranging from high-90-percent to under-10-percent rates, with Google and OpenAI more supportive of economical breach and Anthropic more resistant. Models also responded to specified contractual remedies. The transcript gives no exact model versions, sample sizes or study dates; Rizner's implication is that model choice can alter substantive advice and should be assessed for jurisprudential alignment.
qs: So what we did is we took what were, at the time, the main frontier LLMs — Anthropic, Google, OpenAI — and created large sets of efficient breach scenarios, and tracked how these LLMs would respond to those scenarios.
You might have a swing from high-90-percent breach rates to under-10-percent breach rates depending on what model you were choosing.

The other big note we found is that the LLMs likewise respond to whether you had specific breach remedies within the contract, in a way that a human would also respond to those types of hints within the contract.

I think lawyers need to start thinking about alignment as in: does this particular LLM align with my particular jurisprudential philosophy, or how I would approach this particular question at a more theoretical, more philosophical element of judgment?

kp.k: Junior users risk learning from unsuitable model recommendations
kp.d: Host Marlene Gebauer argues that approved enterprise models can still recommend clauses inconsistent with intended practice, making playbooks, templates or guidance important. She particularly worries about juniors treating drafting tools as learning tools without sufficient experience to reject inappropriate outputs. Anderson agrees and cites junior or new Filevine employees' excessive reliance on frontier-model analyses as an internal observation, not measured evidence about junior lawyers generally.
qs: it just highlights how important it is to have a playbook, or some sort of template or guidance to use in addition to the model
But somebody who’s more junior, and who’s actually using this as a learning tool in addition to a drafting tool, is really going down the wrong path.
some of our employees who are junior at the company or new to the company often rely far too heavily on AI analyses and responses from frontier models

kp.k: Model proliferation could lower costs and expand customization
kp.d: Anderson predicts many specialized models rather than dominance by two or three labs. He reports increased internal use, training and fine-tuning of open-source models, sometimes matching or exceeding frontier capabilities with relatively limited fine-tuning, without supplying benchmark results. He argues that cheaper inference could encourage law firms and other customers to participate in building customized models, while proliferation will also make the market more confusing.
qs: We internally are using more open-source models than ever before — it is now part and parcel of the work we do to fine-tune and train open-source models.
In fact, we’re seeing the open-source models be as good or better, with relatively limited fine-tuning, than even some of what the frontier models can do.
First of all, it means we can use a lot more inference — it’s not as costly as before.
It also means there will probably be a lot more folks — end customers, law firms — choosing to have a stake in helping to build their own models

kp.k: Customized models could disseminate previously tacit firm expertise
kp.d: Rizner predicts “synthetic secondary sources” combining a firm's preferred models and accumulated work-product corpus to reproduce its particular legal approach at scale. He sees this as making knowledge, style and preferences formerly concentrated in partners and senior associates more available. Anderson extends the prediction to individual lawyers and lawyer-client pairings and reports that Filevine already orchestrates multiple models for individual query responses.
qs: with the proliferation of models, you’ll see, increasingly, what I like to call synthetic secondary sources.

it is a technological marriage of our exact corpus with our exact preferred models to get our exact answer, at a scale that’s just not been achievable, because the knowledge and the style and the preferences were locked in the brains of the partner or maybe the senior associates.
It might be the lawyer level, and it might even be the lawyer paired with the client.
We already orchestrate through multiple models just to give you a certain response to a query.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Rizner and Anderson predict that AI will expand legal work, improve research and broaden access rather than replace lawyers; they also anticipate more specialised models and continuing demand for human judgment.
pts.d: John Rizner predicts that easier access to relevant authorities will produce more substantive research, more nuanced arguments and potentially better judicial opinions, rather than merely shorter research time. Ryan Anderson predicts that cheaper drafting and exploration will make previously uneconomic motions and legal theories viable, generating additional litigation and responses from counterparties. He expects increased lawyer capacity to serve previously underserved clients. Rizner argues that the billable hour can survive because time saved on initial production will be reinvested in higher-quality, increasingly partner-level work. On research technology, Rizner claims that LOIS combines citation graphs, semantic retrieval and an LLM-panel process to identify doctrinal conflicts not discoverable through citation links alone. Both speakers argue that human legal judgment remains necessary because plausible outputs can contain fabricated quotations, unsupported propositions or model-specific normative preferences. Rizner reports that model choice can substantially change advice about efficient breach. Anderson anticipates AI use in some consensual private arbitrations, but not near-term replacement of lawyers or judges. He predicts proliferation of models, lower inference costs and greater law-firm participation in customised models. Rizner predicts 'synthetic secondary sources' combining firms’ preferred models with their own knowledge; Anderson extends personalisation to individual lawyers and lawyer–client pairings. Anderson also expects Word to remain a dominant drafting environment and describes an ambition to produce sophisticated long-form documents grounded in evidence and case law. His claims that LOIS has superior precision, retrieval and drafting capabilities are Filevine product claims, not independently established findings in this transcript.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The speakers support their claims with practitioner conversations, company experience, illustrative cases, internal benchmarking and a reported empirical working paper; the market-expansion predictions are not accompanied by quantified legal-market evidence.
pts.d: Rizner bases his research-expansion argument partly on conversations with former law-school classmates who became appellate litigators and wanted more research resources. Anderson offers Filevine’s engineering experience as an analogy: he reports more than tenfold code production, continuing review and testing needs, and an expectation of 400–450 engineers by year-end. He also recounts an engineer implementing a prototype during a meeting and reports customer experiences of LOIS revealing new legal arguments. These are company experiences and anecdotes, not measurements of aggregate legal employment. Anderson’s access argument draws on his brother’s difficulty securing representation in a small real-estate dispute, Filevine’s public-defender and Innocence Project clients, and hypothetical reductions in will-drafting time. Rizner cites quantitative research by Paul Hellyer and Susan Mart on divergence between Lexis and Westlaw, and says Filevine’s current benchmarking still finds substantial divergence; the transcript provides no benchmark sample sizes or scores. He illustrates the proposed retrieval advantage through Brinkerhoff v. Salt Lake City and Standiford, explaining that doctrinal conflict can exist without a direct citation link. Anderson offers a customer example of Claude putting an amalgamation of testimony into quotation marks as evidence for continued human verification. Rizner describes his co-authored working paper, 'The AI’s Philosophy of Contract': scenarios submitted to then-frontier Anthropic, Google and OpenAI models reportedly yielded widely different breach recommendations, with responses also affected by contractual remedies. No exact model versions, sample sizes or statistical details are supplied here. Anderson’s claims about open-source model performance and costs draw on internal fine-tuning experience without published comparative results in the transcript. Both interviewees work for Filevine, whose AI products are central to the discussion and whose commercial interest Anderson explicitly acknowledges.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most forecasts are qualitative and undated: they depend on cheaper, more mature tools, reinvestment of saved time, reliable grounding and continued professional oversight.
pts.d: In this source labelled 2026, Rizner links better research to tools becoming more mature and returning more relevant material, with quality gains developing in the long run. Anderson treats AI adoption as already underway for a couple of years, but acknowledges uncertainty about exactly how access expansion will unfold. Lower client bills depend on tasks requiring less lawyer time even if hourly rates remain stable or increase; the will-drafting figures are illustrative, not measured productivity results. Rizner’s billable-hour prediction is explicitly that it survives 'for a while,' conditional on greater volume and quality absorbing saved time. He expects deeper associate-level nuance both in the very near future and over the long run. Anderson places replacement of lawyers and judges far in the future without a date, and limits his arbitration forecast to small private matters with agreement to AI tooling. Rizner describes citation safeguards as work being built toward, covering case existence, support for the proposition and continuing validity as law; this is not a claim that all three checks have already been solved. The efficient-breach findings concern models available when the study was run, described as research conducted 'this last year,' rather than all future models. Open-source jurisprudential customisation is exploratory. Model proliferation and ultra-customised outputs are near-future forecasts; Anderson says Filevine already uses multiple models and fine-tunes open-source models. Word persistence is expected in the short and probably medium term, while Anderson leaves longer-term re-platforming open.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted effects span litigators, transactional lawyers, junior practitioners, underserved clients, corporate defendants, courts and firms seeking customised legal knowledge.
pts.d: Rizner expects litigators and appellate lawyers to gain broader research coverage and more nuanced arguments. Anderson expects both plaintiffs and defendants to acquire stronger investigative tools, but sees increased litigation as potentially adverse to corporate defendants, including in employment disputes. Lawyers may become busier as cheaper motions generate counterparty responses; judges face a more difficult workload. Anderson identifies family law, immigration, bankruptcy and underrepresented criminal defendants as major beneficiaries of expanded capacity. He anticipates more opportunities for people with meritorious wrongful-prosecution or inadequate-representation claims to obtain relief, and uses wills as an example of serving more clients at lower total cost. These claims concern access to legal help, not merely corporate legal-spend reductions. Associates and partners are expected to use saved time to improve quality, while juniors face both higher expectations and risks of overreliance on model output. Anderson supports the latter concern through observations of junior or newly hired Filevine employees, rather than measured outcomes for junior lawyers. Transactional practitioners are affected by drafting and redlining tools embedded in Word. Firms, individual lawyers and their clients may obtain outputs reflecting their own knowledge, preferences and jurisprudential approaches; model choice could also become contested in AI-assisted arbitration. Filevine is positioned as a legal-technology vendor supplying these tools, not as an alternative provider delivering legal services.
